The state flag depicts the Great Seal of Illinois, which was designed in 1819 and emulated the [Great Seal of the United States](/wiki/Great_Seal_of_the_United_States "Great Seal of the United States"). In the eagle's beak there is a banner with the state motto, "State Sovereignty, National Union." The dates on the seal, 1818 and 1868, represent the year Illinois became a state and the year in which the Great Seal was redesigned by [Sharon Tyndale](/wiki/Sharon_Tyndale "Sharon Tyndale"). Although "State Sovereignty" comes first in the motto, "State" is at the bottom and "Sovereignty" is upside-down.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

It is one of nine U.S. state flags to feature an eagle, alongside those of [Iowa](/wiki/Flag_of_Iowa "Flag of Iowa"), [Michigan](/wiki/Flag_of_Michigan "Flag of Michigan"), [Missouri](/wiki/Flag_of_Missouri "Flag of Missouri"), [New York](/wiki/Coat_of_arms_of_New_York "Coat of arms of New York"), [North Dakota](/wiki/Flag_of_North_Dakota "Flag of North Dakota"), [Oregon](/wiki/Flag_of_Oregon "Flag of Oregon"), [Pennsylvania](/wiki/Flag_of_Pennsylvania "Flag of Pennsylvania"), and [Wyoming](/wiki/Flag_of_Wyoming "Flag of Wyoming").

The earliest [French literature](/wiki/French_literature "French literature") dates from the Middle Ages, when there were several languages and dialects, and writers used their own spelling and grammar. Some authors of medieval texts, such as *[Tristan and Iseult](/wiki/Tristan_and_Iseult "Tristan and Iseult")* and *[Lancelot-Grail](/wiki/Lancelot-Grail "Lancelot-Grail"),* are unknown. Three famous medieval authors are [Chrétien de Troyes](/wiki/Chr%C3%A9tien_de_Troyes "Chrétien de Troyes"), [Christine de Pizan](/wiki/Christine_de_Pizan "Christine de Pizan") ([langue d'oïl](/wiki/Langues_d%27o%C3%AFl "Langues d'oïl")), and Duke [William IX of Aquitaine](/wiki/William_IX_of_Aquitaine "William IX of Aquitaine") ([langue d'oc](/wiki/Occitan_language "Occitan language")). The *Roman de Renart*, written in 1175 by Perrout de Saint Cloude, tells the story of the medieval character [Reynard](/wiki/Reynard_the_Fox "Reynard the Fox") ('the Fox') and is another example of early French writing. It contains over 8,000 different plant species on 1.8 ha (4+1⁄2 acres). It is one of the most diverse yet compact major collections of plants in the world and includes representatives of over 90% of the higher plant families. The [Harcourt Arboretum](/wiki/Harcourt_Arboretum "Harcourt Arboretum") is a 130-acre (53 ha) site six miles (9.7 km) south of the city that includes native woodland and 67 acres (27 hectares) of meadow. The team's logo applies a golden eagle motif to the word "Eagles", which has wings added to its left and right sides. The word "Rakuten" sits at atop in a smaller, simpler font.[[89]](#cite_note-90) The winged "E" from this logo also serves as the team's cap insignia. Starting with the 2020 season, ['47](/wiki/%2747_(brand) "'47 (brand)") supplies the caps for the team. At the start of the 2011 season, [Descente](/wiki/Descente "Descente") provided all of the team's uniforms and apparel.[[91]](#cite_note-92) Then, from 2014 to 2019, the team had a contract with [Majestic Athletic](/wiki/Majestic_Athletic "Majestic Athletic"), the then-supplier of MLB.[[92]](#cite_note-93) Since the start of the 2020 season, [Mizuno Corporation](/wiki/Mizuno_Corporation "Mizuno Corporation") has supplied the uniforms and apparel for the Eagles.[[90]](#cite_note-2020_uniforms-91) The Eagles' uniforms bear the logos of various sponsors on the jersey, pants, cap, and helmet.[[93]](#cite_note-94)

Stuyvesant High School is named after [Peter Stuyvesant](/wiki/Peter_Stuyvesant "Peter Stuyvesant"), the last [Dutch](/wiki/Dutch_Empire "Dutch Empire") governor of [New Netherland](/wiki/New_Netherland "New Netherland") before the colony was transferred to [England](/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") in 1664.[[2]](#cite_note-StuyLandmark-2) Of the nine Specialized high schools, Stuyvesant has the highest score cutoff for entry.

The school was established in 1904 as a [manual training school](/wiki/Vocational_education "Vocational education") for boys, hosting 155 students and 12 teachers. Most of Oregon has a generally mild climate, though there is significant variation given the variety of landscapes across the state.[[89]](#cite_note-91) The state's western region (west of the [Cascade Range](/wiki/Cascade_Range "Cascade Range")) has an [oceanic climate](/wiki/Oceanic_climate "Oceanic climate"), populated by dense [evergreen](/wiki/Temperate_rainforest "Temperate rainforest") mixed forests. Western Oregon's climate is heavily influenced by the Pacific Ocean; the western third of Oregon is very wet in the winter, moderately to very wet during the spring and fall, and dry during the summer. The [relative humidity](/wiki/Relative_humidity "Relative humidity") of Western Oregon is high except during summer days, which are semi-dry to semi-humid; Eastern Oregon typically sees low humidity year-round.[[90]](#cite_note-dri-92)

The state's southwestern portion, particularly the [Rogue Valley](/wiki/Rogue_Valley "Rogue Valley"), has a [Mediterranean climate](/wiki/Mediterranean_climate "Mediterranean climate") with drier and sunnier winters and hotter summers, similar to [Northern California](/wiki/Northern_California "Northern California").[[91]](#cite_note-93)

The timing of "fire season" in California is variable, depending on the amount of prior winter and spring precipitation, the frequency and severity of weather such as heat waves and wind events, and moisture content in vegetation. [Northern California](/wiki/Northern_California "Northern California") typically sees wildfire activity between late spring and early fall, peaking in the summer with hotter and drier conditions. Occasional cold frontal passages can bring wind and lightning. The timing of fire season in Southern California is similar, peaking between late spring and fall. The severity and duration of peak activity in either part of the state is modulated in part by weather events: downslope/offshore wind events can lead to critical fire weather, while onshore flow and Pacific weather systems can bring conditions that hamper wildfire growth.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-:02-5)

The **Yellow River**,[[a]](#cite_note-1) also known as **Huanghe**, is the [second-longest river](/wiki/List_of_the_longest_rivers_of_China "List of the longest rivers of China") in China and the [sixth-longest](/wiki/List_of_rivers_by_length "List of rivers by length") river system on Earth, with an estimated length of 5,464 km (3,395 mi) and a [drainage basin](/wiki/Drainage_basin "Drainage basin") of 795,000 km2 (307,000 sq mi). Beginning in the [Bayan Har Mountains](/wiki/Bayan_Har_Mountains "Bayan Har Mountains"), the river flows generally eastwards before entering the 1,500 km (930 mi) long Ordos Loop, which runs northeast at [Gansu](/wiki/Gansu "Gansu") through the [Ordos Plateau](/wiki/Ordos_Plateau "Ordos Plateau") and turns east in [Inner Mongolia](/wiki/Inner_Mongolia "Inner Mongolia"). The river then turns sharply southwards to form the border between [Shanxi](/wiki/Shanxi "Shanxi") and [Shaanxi](/wiki/Shaanxi "Shaanxi"), turns eastwards at its confluence with the [Wei River](/wiki/Wei_River "Wei River"), and flows across the [North China Plain](/wiki/North_China_Plain "North China Plain") before emptying into the [Bohai Sea](/wiki/Bohai_Sea "Bohai Sea"). The river is named for the yellow color of its water, which comes from the large amount of sediment discharged into the water as the river flows through the [Loess Plateau](/wiki/Loess_Plateau "Loess Plateau").[[1]](#cite_note-:022-2)

The Yellow River basin was the birthplace of [ancient Chinese civilization](/wiki/Yellow_River_civilization "Yellow River civilization"). According to traditional [Chinese historiography](/wiki/Chinese_historiography "Chinese historiography"), the [Xia dynasty](/wiki/Xia_dynasty "Xia dynasty") originated on its banks around 2100 BC; [Sima Qian](/wiki/Sima_Qian "Sima Qian")'s *[Shiji](/wiki/Shiji "Shiji")* (c. 91 BC) record that the Xia were founded after the tribes around the Yellow River united to combat the frequent floods in the area. The river has provided fertile soil for agriculture, but since then has flooded and changed course frequently, with one estimate counting 1,593 floods in the 2,540 years between 595 BC and 1946 AD

Increasing demand for boric acid has led a number of producers to invest in additional capacity.
